status: Complete proposed coverage map. Actual lesson availability and technical verification are recorded in integration.json and lesson-audits.json; planned coverage alone is not completed instruction.
use: Every lesson requires original instruction, stated notation and domains, worked reasoning, guided feedback, an accessible investigation, deterministic practice and a checkpoint. The entries below specify subject-specific coverage and evidence; assessments.json and verification.json add the shared release conditions. Family names describe intended coverage; integration.json and lesson-audits.json record actual availability and checks.

lessons.title: Harmonic motion, phase and initial conditions
lessons.objective: Reconstruct and check a harmonic trajectory from physical parameters or initial conditions, including phase, direction and admissible event times.
coverage: Restoring force and the equation x''=-omega²x
Period, frequency, angular frequency and radians
Position, velocity and acceleration as related functions
Amplitude and phase from x(0),v(0), with quadrant and zero-amplitude cases
Position crossings, turning points, repeated solutions and requested time windows
Phase-space ellipse and dimensional checks
examples: A 0.5 kg mass on an 8 N/m spring starts at x=0.03 m with v=-0.16 m/s; derive A=0.05 m and the correct phase, then verify both initial conditions.
Find the first positive return and the opposite-direction crossing; distinguish a full state recurrence from a repeated position.
Compare an unchanged physical trajectory written with two equivalent phases and a shift of the time origin.
misconceptions: Using frequency in place of angular frequency
Choosing phase with arccos alone and losing velocity direction
Equating zero velocity with zero acceleration
Giving only a principal trigonometric root
lessons.investigation: Keyboard-controlled time probe with synchronized x, v, a and phase-plane views; predict a sign or crossing before revealing it. Numeric table and state descriptions provide the full alternative to plots. Sampling changes must expose aliasing rather than suggest a changed physical frequency.
lessons.independentChecks: Verify states with a 2 by 2 rotation matrix, both initial conditions and x²+(v/omega)²=A². Enumerate roots independently in bounded time intervals. Include zero amplitude, t=0 exclusions, negative initial position and velocity, and equivalent phases.

lessons.title: Energy, physical oscillators and stable equilibrium
lessons.objective: Derive a local oscillation model from force, torque or potential energy and assess its frequency and small-amplitude limits.
coverage: Exchange between kinetic and spring energy
Shift of equilibrium under constant force
Effective stiffness and U'' at stable or unstable equilibria
Simple, physical and torsional pendulums
Parallel/series springs and effective inertia
Small-angle approximation and amplitude-dependent period limits
examples: Separate a vertical spring's static extension from its oscillation amplitude and period.
Derive a uniform rod pendulum's small-angle period about an end from I and center-of-mass torque.
Use a quartic potential to locate equilibria and compare local curvature without calling a negative-curvature point an oscillator.
misconceptions: Adding mg to the restoring stiffness
Confusing potential curvature with potential height
Using a point-mass pendulum formula for a rigid body
Treating small-angle error as zero
lessons.investigation: Compare linearized and nonlinear pendulum trajectories at controlled initial angles, using identical integration resolution and an energy diagnostic. Plot period estimates with a table of crossing times and convergence evidence.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate force to potential, differentiate the potential back, and check energy at independently chosen phases. Use analytic small-angle periods and converged quadrature of the nonlinear pendulum period; reject impossible energies or negative inertia.

lessons.title: Free decay and damping regimes
lessons.objective: Classify and solve a damped oscillator's initial-value response and distinguish amplitude, energy and settling measures.
coverage: Viscous damping coefficient units
Characteristic roots and underdamped, critical and overdamped responses
Damped versus natural frequency
Initial-condition constants and signed zero crossings
Peak ratios and logarithmic decrement
Dissipated power, energy balance and limits of an exponential energy envelope
examples: Use m=1 kg, k=25 N/m and b=6 kg/s to derive decaying oscillation with damped frequency 4 rad/s.
Compare b=10 and b=12 with the same initial displacement; retain the critical repeated-root term.
Infer a damping rate from separated positive peaks and state which model assumptions support it.
misconceptions: Using the underdamped formula at every damping value
Replacing instantaneous energy by its envelope
Assuming critical damping minimizes every possible settling definition
lessons.investigation: Compare all three regimes with common initial conditions and tabulated displacement, velocity, energy and accumulated dissipation. Peak picking and a stated settling band reveal why the chosen measurement matters.
lessons.independentChecks: Compare analytic roots against an independently implemented matrix-exponential or high-accuracy ODE reference. Check E'= -b v² and continuity approaching critical damping; test b=0, both signs of initial velocity and near-repeated roots.

lessons.title: Driven response, resonance and power transfer
lessons.objective: Predict a driven oscillator's steady amplitude, phase and average power while separating transient behavior and distinct resonance criteria.
coverage: Sinusoidal forcing and transient plus steady solution
Amplitude and phase with a quadrant-aware denominator
Low/high-frequency limits
Displacement, velocity and power resonance
Quality factor and the domain of narrow-band approximations
Cycle work, average dissipation and undamped resonant growth
examples: Compare forcing below, at and above the natural frequency with fixed force amplitude.
Find a displacement peak that differs from the velocity/power peak, including damping too large for a nonzero displacement peak.
Explain why an undamped resonant drive has no bounded sinusoidal steady state.
misconceptions: Calling every peak omega0
Treating steady state as the initial response
Losing phase quadrants
Letting a zero damping denominator yield an ordinary finite answer
lessons.investigation: Frequency sweep with displacement, velocity and average-power curves; select a measured output before predicting its peak. A time trace and complete table distinguish startup from settled cycles.
lessons.independentChecks: Substitute complex or real sine/cosine coefficients into the differential equation, integrate work over an integer cycle, and independently differentiate the squared amplitude to find admissible maxima.

lessons.title: Wave functions and transport of energy
lessons.objective: Interpret a traveling wave's direction, local motion and energy transport using its derivatives and medium parameters.
coverage: Transverse and longitudinal disturbances
Travel direction from constant phase
Wave number, wavelength, frequency and phase speed
Partial derivatives and the one-dimensional wave equation
String tension and linear mass density
Local particle velocity versus propagation speed
Energy density and average string-wave power
examples: Differentiate y(x,t)=A cos(kx-omega t+phi) at a fixed position and follow one crest separately.
Infer a string's wave speed and average power from tension, density and amplitude.
Test a proposed function against a stated wave equation rather than recognizing its shape alone.
misconceptions: Identifying particle speed with wave speed
Reading direction from a snapshot
Treating average power as proportional to amplitude
lessons.investigation: Move position and time probes independently on a wave; compare crest motion with a tagged medium point. A derivative table, energy account and controllable sample spacing are available without animation.
lessons.independentChecks: Use shifted-profile transport and symbolic derivatives, not the displayed graph generator. Verify energy flux equals speed times mean energy density for the ideal string and test both travel directions.

lessons.title: Superposition, reflection and normal modes
lessons.objective: Construct superposed waves that satisfy boundary conditions and identify their nodes, allowed modes and energy behavior.
coverage: Linear superposition and coherent phase
Fixed/free reflection signs and transmitted amplitude
Standing waves as counter-propagating traveling waves
Fixed-fixed and mixed boundary spectra
Nodes versus instants of zero displacement
Two identical coupled oscillators and symmetric/antisymmetric modes
Beat envelopes and mode superposition limits
examples: Derive allowed wavelengths on a fixed-fixed string and a mixed-boundary string.
Superpose equal counter-propagating waves and locate permanent nodes.
Check two coupled masses' in-phase and out-of-phase motions directly against their two force equations.
misconceptions: A standing wave transports the same net power as one traveling constituent
Every zero in one frame is a node
Intensity always adds for coherent sources
Every boundary has the same harmonic series
lessons.investigation: Choose boundary conditions and excite modes; compare a node probe, snapshots and constituent powers. A two-mass panel connects mode shapes to the continuum pattern using numeric tables and keyboard steps.
lessons.independentChecks: Substitute endpoint conditions, integrate flux over a cycle, and diagonalize only the explicit two-by-two coupled system in the test reference. Include cancellation, unequal amplitudes and prohibited mode numbers.

lessons.title: Sound, intensity and moving sources
lessons.objective: Relate pressure waves and sound measurements to intensity, interference and relative source-observer motion within a stated medium.
coverage: Pressure and displacement phase relation
Acoustic speed and the limited ideal-gas model
Intensity, inverse-square spreading and decibel reference
Coherent versus incoherent combination
Open/closed air-column boundary conditions
Beats and classical Doppler signs
Subsonic domain and shock-cone extension
examples: Convert an intensity ratio into a level difference without adding decibels directly.
Separate a moving source from a moving observer relative to stationary air.
Compare pressure nodes and displacement antinodes at an ideal open end.
misconceptions: Decibels are an absolute linear intensity
Source and observer speeds are interchangeable
Frequency and wave speed both change for a moving listener
lessons.investigation: A spacetime wavefront diagram and arrival-time table compare source and observer motion. Synthetic level and beat measurements show the effect of reference and coherence. No loud audio is required or emitted automatically.
lessons.independentChecks: Calculate consecutive arrival times geometrically before comparing with the Doppler formula. Verify inverse-square ratios, pressure/intensity units and log conversions; reject zero or negative classical denominators.

lessons.title: Charge, force and the electric field
lessons.objective: Calculate signed vector electric forces and fields from discrete sources and distinguish source properties from the response of a test charge.
coverage: Charge conservation and quantization
Conductors, insulators and induction
Coulomb's law with source-to-observation vectors
Three-dimensional superposition
Field versus force and test-charge sign
Dipole moment, torque and the far-field limit
Field-line interpretation without literal trajectories
examples: Sum the field from positive and negative charges at an off-axis point before multiplying by the test charge.
Locate a zero-field point and reject a root outside the assumed region.
Compare an exact two-charge dipole calculation with its large-distance approximation.
misconceptions: Field direction changes when the test charge changes
Adding force magnitudes instead of components
Treating field lines as material paths
lessons.investigation: Move discrete sources and a probe using number inputs or keyboard steps. Predict vector signs before revealing components, force and a source-contribution table; singular observation points are excluded explicitly.
lessons.independentChecks: Use separately constructed displacement vectors and pairwise force antisymmetry. Check scaling with distance and charge, symmetry cancellation and exact-versus-dipole residuals.

lessons.title: Fields of continuous charge distributions
lessons.objective: Set up and evaluate electric-field integrals with correct density, geometry, vector direction and admissible observation points.
coverage: Line, surface and volume density units
Source and observation coordinates
Finite rods, arcs, rings and axial disks
Symmetry cancellation before integration
Nonuniform density and total-charge normalization
Numerical quadrature for general distributions
Far-field, infinite-source and near-source limits
examples: Integrate the field on a uniformly charged ring's axis and check the center and far field.
Compute an axial disk field by adding rings, keeping the signed side of the disk.
Compare a nonuniform finite rod's exact integral with successively refined midpoint sums.
misconceptions: Pulling a varying distance outside an integral
Using the wrong differential charge
Replacing every extended source by a point at its center
lessons.investigation: Refine a source discretization and compare component sums with analytic special cases. Report cell size, nearest-source distance and convergence; never hide a singular point behind a softening parameter.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate with a separately implemented adaptive rule, compare analytic ring/disk/rod formulas, and test dimensional density conversions and total charge. Include both sides of a plane and finite-domain edge points.

lessons.title: Electric flux and the proper use of Gauss's law
lessons.objective: Calculate oriented flux and use Gauss's law to determine a field only when the source symmetry supports the required reduction.
coverage: Oriented area and flux through open and closed surfaces
Enclosed versus external charge
Spherical, cylindrical and planar symmetry
Piecewise fields inside and outside nonconducting distributions
Uniform versus varying volume density
Gaussian surfaces are mathematical boundaries
Why an integral law does not always determine the local field
examples: Calculate flux through each face of a box in a nonuniform field and infer net enclosed charge.
Derive a charged solid sphere's interior and exterior fields, including continuity.
Explain why an off-center source prevents a simple E times area substitution on a chosen sphere.
misconceptions: Zero flux means zero field
Only enclosed charges contribute to the field
E is automatically constant on any Gaussian surface
lessons.investigation: Compare face-resolved flux and enclosed charge while moving an external source. Symmetric and asymmetric cases share a flux table but expose different local field patterns.
lessons.independentChecks: Numerically integrate surface flux independently of the field solver and integrate density over volume. Check r=0 limits, interface continuity and exterior inverse-square behavior.

lessons.title: Conductors, cavities and electrostatic boundaries
lessons.objective: Determine charge allocation and field constraints in electrostatic conductors while distinguishing metal, cavities and surrounding space.
coverage: Electrostatic equilibrium versus a current-carrying conductor
Zero interior metal field and tangential surface field
Surface-charge jump in normal field
Induced charge on cavity and exterior surfaces
Isolated versus grounded conductors
Shielding limits and charged cavities
Concentric spherical examples and nonspherical local-field limits
examples: Place charge q inside a cavity of an isolated conductor with total charge Q and derive inner and outer net charges.
Distinguish an empty shielded cavity from a cavity containing an off-center charge.
Use a pillbox to relate an exterior normal field to local surface density without assuming uniform density.
misconceptions: A conductor's cavity is always field-free
Grounding means every conductor surface has zero charge
Uniform net charge implies uniform local density
lessons.investigation: A region and charge-account explorer compares isolated/grounded spherical shells and off-center qualitative cases. Accessible tables identify what Gauss's law determines and what remains unknown.
lessons.independentChecks: Use charge conservation plus Gaussian surfaces lying inside metal, with separately derived region fields in spherical fixtures. Keep net-charge conclusions distinct from unsupported local distributions.

lessons.title: Potential, work and field reconstruction
lessons.objective: Connect electrostatic field and potential through line integrals and gradients, retaining reference choices and source-domain restrictions.
coverage: Potential difference, potential energy and external work
Finite charge sums and continuous-source potential integrals
Reference at infinity when the integral converges
Finite reference differences for infinite lines and planes
Gradient components and equipotential geometry
Gauge shifts and unchanged physics
Path independence and its electrostatic boundary
examples: Obtain the potential of a charged ring on its axis and differentiate it to recover the field.
Compute a line-charge potential difference without assigning zero potential at infinity.
Differentiate a two-variable polynomial potential and compare work along two paths.
misconceptions: V=0 implies E=0
Potential and potential energy are interchangeable
Every source permits V(infinity)=0
lessons.investigation: Compare two integration paths, a potential contour map and numerical gradient vectors; an additive gauge changes values but not forces. Tables expose integration error and source exclusions.
lessons.independentChecks: Differentiate independently derived scalar potentials and perform separate path quadrature. Check a finite gauge change, negative charges and paths near excluded source points.

lessons.title: Capacitance, networks and stored energy
lessons.objective: Determine capacitance, charge, voltage and energy for specified geometries and connected capacitors, with topology and source conditions explicit.
coverage: Capacitance as a geometry/material relation
Parallel plate, coaxial and spherical geometries
Series and parallel conservation constraints
Equivalent capacitance versus individual energy
Charging work and one-half QV
Isolated redistribution and missing energy
Fringing and idealization limits
examples: Derive coaxial capacitance by integrating the radial field between the conductors.
Resolve a mixed three-capacitor network and check every node charge and voltage sum.
Connect two isolated charged capacitors and account for the decrease in electrostatic energy.
misconceptions: Series capacitors have equal voltages
Capacitance grows just because more charge is supplied
Lost stored energy violates conservation
lessons.investigation: Switch between stated capacitor connections and source-connected/isolated states. Predict charge and energy before seeing a complete component table and conservation residuals.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate field energy over the geometry and compare with one-half CV². Solve charge/voltage constraints independently and audit dimensions, limiting separations and redistribution energy.

lessons.title: Dielectrics and electromechanical energy accounting
lessons.objective: Predict a capacitor's response to dielectric or geometry changes by distinguishing fixed charge, fixed voltage and the work of external sources.
coverage: Polarization and bound versus free charge
Linear dielectric constant and breakdown limits
Fixed-Q and fixed-V changes
Partially filled capacitors and interface geometry
Source work, field-energy change and mechanical work
Electrostatic force from a consistent energy account
Uncertainty in thickness, permittivity and measured capacitance
examples: Insert a dielectric into disconnected and battery-connected capacitors and compare Q,V,E and U.
Combine dielectric layers perpendicular or parallel to the field and justify the equivalent network.
Find insertion force at fixed voltage while including battery work, avoiding the wrong sign from field energy alone.
misconceptions: Dielectric insertion always reduces stored energy
Free and bound charge are the same account
Differentiating field energy alone is valid at fixed voltage
lessons.investigation: An ideal capacitor energy ledger compares source and isolation controls, dielectric insertion and geometric uncertainty. Results are synthetic and do not authorize testing breakdown or handling charged hardware.
lessons.independentChecks: Compute charge and source work separately, use virtual work with the appropriate controlled quantity, and bracket monotone parameter uncertainties. Test zero insertion, identical media and both source states.

lessons.title: Current density, resistance and material response
lessons.objective: Relate charge transport to current, local fields, resistance and heating while identifying the limits of an ohmic material model.
coverage: Current as a rate and density as a vector flux
Carrier density, signed drift and conventional current
Microscopic versus macroscopic Ohm relations
Resistance of uniform and nonuniform conductors
Resistivity and restricted temperature models
Electrical power and energy
Non-ohmic IV data and instrument resolution
examples: Integrate a radially varying current density through a circular cross-section.
Compare wire resistance after changing length and area at constant material volume.
Use synthetic IV readings to reject a constant-resistance fit outside its stated range.
misconceptions: Charge is consumed in a resistor
Resistance and resistivity have the same units
Ohm's law is universal
Electron drift equals signal speed
lessons.investigation: Explore geometry and synthetic IV curves with a fitted slope, power column and residual bounds. Temperature is a stated input or a specified thermal model, not an unexplained automatic correction.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate density and resistivity directly, compare electrical work with charge times voltage, and test area scaling, sign reversal and endpoint uncertainty without circular use of displayed fits.

lessons.title: DC circuit constraints and instrument loading
lessons.objective: Solve a DC network with signed current and voltage references, verify power balance, and predict how a real meter changes the circuit.
coverage: Emf, terminal voltage and internal resistance
Topology, nodes and series/parallel criteria
Kirchhoff current and loop equations
Two-loop systems and negative current results
Voltmeters, ammeters and loading
Open/short limits and impossible ideal-source connections
Circuit energy and steady charge conservation
examples: Solve a two-source two-loop network and interpret a negative branch current.
Calculate voltage-divider loading by a finite-input-resistance meter.
Check whether a source delivers or absorbs power under the chosen reference convention.
misconceptions: An emf is a mechanical force
A negative current makes a solution invalid
A voltmeter has no effect
Geometric appearance alone determines series connection
lessons.investigation: Switch a finite meter into a fixed, clearly labeled circuit and compare predictions with node/branch tables. Solve and show charge/power residuals. Schematic nodes have an equivalent connection list.
lessons.independentChecks: Use a separately assembled nodal conductance matrix and branch power sum. Include source opposition, disconnected branches and finite meter limits. Do not model inconsistent ideal voltage sources as a numeric finite solution.

lessons.title: RC switching, initial conditions and time scales
lessons.objective: Derive and check a first-order circuit transient with a specified pre-switch state, final value and admissible switching model.
coverage: Capacitor voltage continuity under finite current
Effective resistance seen after switching
General exponential approach to a nonzero final value
Signed current and power during charging/discharging
Threshold times and unreachable targets
Energy dissipated and supplied
Measured traces, time resolution and fitting limits
examples: Switch a precharged capacitor to a different source and calculate voltage and current immediately and later.
Solve a settling threshold using a logarithm with its domain checked.
Compare capacitor-energy change with source work and resistor heating.
misconceptions: A capacitor is always an open circuit
Voltage changes instantaneously through finite resistance
One time constant means complete charging
Every requested threshold is reached
lessons.investigation: A switch-state explorer compares analytic traces with numerical integration and synthetic sampled measurements; a table includes capacitor voltage, current and accumulated energy terms. Restore the chosen state on reload.
lessons.independentChecks: Solve the linear ODE independently and integrate resistor power analytically. Check t=0 and long time, signed initial differences, zero response and parameter bounds.

lessons.title: Lorentz force and charged-particle motion
lessons.objective: Predict charged-particle force and trajectory in specified uniform fields with consistent vector signs and energy reasoning.
coverage: Magnetic-field units and oriented cross products
Lorentz force with electric and magnetic terms
Circular and helical motion
Signed curvature, radius, period and pitch
Velocity selectors and crossed fields
Magnetic force does no instantaneous work
Nonrelativistic and uniform-field limits
examples: Find force and curvature for positive and negative charges with the same initial velocity.
Decompose helical motion into parallel and perpendicular velocity.
Derive a velocity selector's condition and show which charges are deflected when speed changes.
misconceptions: Magnetic force changes speed in a static magnetic field
Radius uses the total helical speed
Right-hand direction ignores charge sign
lessons.investigation: A stepped 3D trajectory with vector components and a state table compares charge sign and field orientation. Energy and parallel velocity serve as visible invariants; no color or motion cue is the sole explanation.
lessons.independentChecks: Use analytic rotation of perpendicular velocity and a dot-product work test. Include parallel and zero velocity, negative charge, zero field and explicitly rejected relativistic use.

lessons.title: Currents, magnetic dipoles and material models
lessons.objective: Calculate force, torque and energy for current-carrying conductors and magnetic dipoles while identifying the assumptions of simple material models.
coverage: Force integral on a current-carrying wire
Closed loops in uniform and nonuniform fields
Magnetic moment, torque and orientation energy
Stable and unstable dipole orientations
Parallel-current force
Diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic distinctions
Linear permeability, hysteresis and saturation limits
examples: Sum forces on a rectangular loop in a uniform field and derive its torque.
Compare dipole energy at aligned and opposed orientations.
Read a supplied hysteresis loop and distinguish a local slope model from a single universal permeability.
misconceptions: Zero net force means zero torque
Every magnetic material has constant permeability
A dipole feels no force in a field gradient
lessons.investigation: Change loop orientation and a supplied field gradient, with component forces and torque tables. A synthetic material curve makes model range and hysteresis history explicit.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate force segment by segment and calculate torque about two origins when net force is zero. Differentiate dipole energy and compare with torque; material data checks remain within the supplied model range.

lessons.title: Biot-Savart, Ampere's law and magnetic geometry
lessons.objective: Compute magnetostatic fields from currents and justify when a circulation law can determine their spatial dependence.
coverage: Biot-Savart vector integrals
Finite and infinite straight wires
Circular loop axis and superposition
Ampere circulation and enclosed signed current
Solenoids, toroids and long-device approximations
Fields inside extended current distributions
Limits of magnetostatic symmetry arguments
examples: Integrate the field on a loop axis and check its center and far-field behavior.
Derive the interior and exterior field of a wire with a stated radial current density.
Contrast an ideal infinite solenoid with a finite-axis field calculation.
misconceptions: Zero enclosed current guarantees zero field
Ampere's law supplies constant B on any loop
A finite solenoid has exactly zero exterior field
lessons.investigation: Compare line-integral circulation with sampled local fields for symmetric and asymmetric current layouts. A source-segment refinement table is available beside the vector plot.
lessons.independentChecks: Use independent segment quadrature and analytic special cases; check right-hand orientation, signed circulation, interface limits and scaling with current.

lessons.title: Changing flux and induced electric fields
lessons.objective: Calculate signed induced emf for a specified circuit and distinguish transformer induction, motional emf and electrostatic potential difference.
coverage: Loop/normal orientation and magnetic flux
Faraday and Lenz signs
Changing field, area or orientation
Motional emf and magnetic force on charges
Nonconservative induced electric fields
Moving rods, loops and energy conversion
Piecewise entry/exit and assumptions behind the flux rule
examples: Determine emf and current sign in a loop with increasing flux using a declared normal.
Move a rod through a uniform field and balance mechanical input with resistor heating.
Compare two voltmeter paths in a changing magnetic field without assigning one global scalar potential.
misconceptions: Induced current always opposes the magnetic field
Emf is flux rather than its rate
A nonconservative field has path-independent voltage
lessons.investigation: Control a loop's motion through a finite field region and inspect signed flux, emf, current, force and power. A static table covers every transition; moving geometry and sign conventions remain explicit.
lessons.independentChecks: Differentiate independently constructed flux histories, integrate Lorentz force along a moving rod, and compare mechanical work with electrical dissipation. Check zero rate and reversal of both loop/normal conventions.

lessons.title: Inductance, coupled coils and RL transients
lessons.objective: Relate current to flux linkage, stored magnetic energy and inductive voltage, including mutual coupling and initial-value circuit behavior.
coverage: Flux linkage versus one-turn flux
Self and mutual inductance with polarity conventions
Energy and the bound on mutual coupling
Linear inductor voltage and current continuity
RL rise/decay with nonzero initial current
Field energy density and solenoid inductance
Switching-model limits and back-emf
examples: Derive a long solenoid's inductance and compare circuit and field energy.
Solve an RL switch to a new source while retaining the pre-switch current.
Audit whether supplied L1,L2,M values permit nonnegative stored energy for all currents.
misconceptions: Inductor current jumps through a finite voltage
Mutual-inductance sign is independent of terminal references
Any arbitrarily large M is physically admissible
lessons.investigation: A coupled-coil energy table and RL transient explorer show current continuity, voltage polarity and energy flow. The model rejects an indefinite inductance matrix and incompatible ideal switch states.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate magnetic energy independently and inspect the two-coil quadratic form at extreme current ratios. Verify the RL solution by substitution and analytic dissipation integration.

lessons.title: Generators, transformers and transmission losses
lessons.objective: Build a power account for idealized generators and transformers and evaluate the assumptions behind voltage conversion and reduced line losses.
coverage: Generator emf from rotating flux linkage
Back-emf and electromechanical power
Ideal transformer turns, voltage and current ratios
Reflected resistance and power conservation
Specified winding/core losses and efficiency
Transmission current and I²R loss
Frequency, saturation and steady-DC limitations
examples: Derive a rotating coil's sinusoidal emf amplitude from its geometry and speed.
Reflect a resistive load through an ideal transformer and account for both currents.
Compare line losses at two transmission voltages while retaining the same delivered power and stated line model.
misconceptions: A transformer creates power
Steady DC can be transformed indefinitely by the AC model
Increasing voltage eliminates all losses
lessons.investigation: A simulation-only source-transformer-line-load ledger varies turns ratio and specified losses. Accessible tables show input, delivered power and residuals; no mains wiring or physical transformer construction is assigned.
lessons.independentChecks: Differentiate flux directly, compare torque times angular speed with electrical power, and independently solve the resistive equivalent circuit. Check passive losses, zero load and infeasible requested delivery.

lessons.title: Sinusoids, phasors and impedance
lessons.objective: Translate between time-domain sinusoids and complex phasors to solve a linear sinusoidal circuit with consistent amplitude and phase conventions.
coverage: Peak and RMS conventions
Real-part exp(j omega t) representation
Derivative and integral correspondence
Resistive, capacitive and inductive impedances
Series and parallel complex combinations
Reference phases, quadrants and physical real signals
Validity only at one frequency in steady linear response
examples: Convert a sine-based voltage into the stated cosine phasor convention.
Solve a series RLC current and component voltages, then reconstruct a time-domain waveform.
Compare a parallel admittance calculation with direct branch-current sums.
misconceptions: A phasor is a physical complex-valued voltage
RMS and peak amplitudes can be mixed
Impedance magnitudes add as scalars
All phase angles come from a one-quadrant arctangent
lessons.investigation: A phasor diagram synchronized with static time samples exposes reference rotation, component phase and complex sums. All vectors have a rectangular/polar table and keyboard inputs.
lessons.independentChecks: Solve sine/cosine coefficients directly without the production complex helpers, then compare sampled real signals and Kirchhoff residuals. Test pure R,L,C limits and zero-valued phase ambiguity.

lessons.title: Electrical oscillation and resonance evidence
lessons.objective: Relate free LC/RLC transients to driven resonance and interpret the measured response, damping and bandwidth for a specified output.
coverage: LC exchange of magnetic and electric energy
RLC natural modes and mechanical analogy
Series driven-current resonance
Component-voltage peaks and output-dependent resonance
Quality factor and bandwidth with stated definitions
Transient versus swept steady response
Component tolerances and parasitic loss
examples: Derive an LC oscillation from initial capacitor charge and inductor current.
Compare current and capacitor-voltage peaks in a damped series circuit.
Infer component or loss information from a frequency sweep while identifying what resonance alone cannot determine.
misconceptions: Every circuit output peaks at the same frequency
A resonance frequency separately identifies both L and C
A fast sweep is automatically steady state
lessons.investigation: Sweep frequency or step the time response with explicit settling conditions. Peak, half-power and component-voltage tables support quantitative comparisons and uncertainty bounds.
lessons.independentChecks: Use the differential-equation state matrix for transients and independently differentiated transfer-function magnitudes for peak conditions. Check cycle energy balance and exact half-power roots before using a high-Q approximation.

lessons.title: Average power, RMS and power factor
lessons.objective: Compute real energy transfer and distinguish it from reactive exchange and apparent power under stated waveform and reference conditions.
coverage: Instantaneous power and cycle averaging
RMS from its defining integral
Complex power with the conjugate convention
Real, reactive and apparent power units
Leading/lagging current and power factor
Reactive compensation and unchanged real load power
Nonsinusoidal waveforms and limits of cosine-only power factor
examples: Integrate the product of sinusoidal voltage and current and recover Vrms Irms cos(phi).
Separate real and reactive power for an RLC load and verify resistor heating.
Compare true power factor with phase displacement for a supplied non-sinusoidal current.
misconceptions: Reactive power is net energy consumed per cycle
Apparent power equals real power
RMS is always peak divided by square root of two
Compensation removes the real energy demand
lessons.investigation: A waveform and power ledger compares resistive, inductive, capacitive and explicitly harmonic cases. Numeric integration, sample refinement and tables provide the answer independent of the plotted area.
lessons.independentChecks: Perform separate exact or high-resolution time integration and compare with complex-power calculations. Test the bound |P|<=Vrms Irms, purely reactive loads, reference reversal and non-sinusoidal counterexamples.

lessons.title: Maxwell's equations and charge continuity
lessons.objective: Use integral field laws to check charge continuity and displacement current, and interpret their local differential forms with stated material assumptions.
coverage: Four vacuum field equations in integral form
Divergence and curl through flux/circulation limits
Continuity equation and charge conservation
Displacement current in a charging capacitor
Two spanning surfaces with one common loop
Electrostatic and magnetostatic limits
Material and boundary qualifications
examples: Calculate the same magnetic circulation using a wire-cutting surface and a capacitor-gap surface.
Integrate a supplied current-density divergence to find a charge-accumulation rate.
Check a proposed field's curl and divergence against its stated sources.
misconceptions: Displacement current is charge crossing a vacuum gap
Gauss's magnetic law says magnetic fields vanish
Static versions of the laws cover every changing field
lessons.investigation: Compare surfaces spanning a charging-capacitor loop and track conduction, displacement and total current. A source/field ledger and local derivative table expose inconsistent field proposals.
lessons.independentChecks: Compute volume and surface balances by separate integrals and check analytic derivatives of polynomial field fixtures. Preserve oriented signs and compare both capacitor surfaces.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic wave solutions and polarization
lessons.objective: Construct a plane electromagnetic wave consistent with Maxwell's equations and interpret its direction, polarization and medium-dependent speed.
coverage: Vacuum wave equation from coupled curl equations
Transverse E,B and propagation orientation
E/B ratio and consistent constants
Linear and circular polarization from component phase
Homogeneous linear medium and constitutive assumptions
Frequency, wavelength and phase speed across a boundary
Spectrum categories without assigning a false material medium to vacuum waves
examples: Construct B for an E wave traveling in a stated positive or negative axis direction.
Show how two orthogonal electric components with a phase difference determine polarization.
Calculate wavelength change across a nondispersive interface while frequency remains fixed.
misconceptions: E and B are parallel
Field direction alone fixes propagation direction
All media have vacuum E/B ratio
Wave frequency changes merely because speed changes
lessons.investigation: Step a plane wave in time with vector arrows, component traces and an orientation table. Change phase and medium assumptions; a consistency check uses both curl laws and the direction of E cross B.
lessons.independentChecks: Differentiate both fields analytically, check the two curl equations and zero divergences, and use an independent cross product to verify propagation. Include sign-reversed waves and degenerate polarization.

lessons.title: Field energy, intensity and radiation pressure
lessons.objective: Account for energy and momentum carried by electromagnetic waves and distinguish local fields, average intensity and material interaction models.
coverage: Electric and magnetic energy density
Poynting vector and its time average
Power through an oriented aperture
Absorption, reflection and momentum transfer
Radiation pressure for stated incidence models
Polarizer transmission and coherent superposition
Inverse-square spreading, near-field and material-loss limits
examples: Compute a plane wave's mean intensity from peak E and separately from mean energy density.
Compare absorbed and perfectly reflected normal-incidence momentum flux.
Apply two ideal polarizers in sequence and distinguish unpolarized input from a known linear state.
misconceptions: Peak and average intensity are interchangeable
A perfectly reflecting surface absorbs all incident energy
Near fields always obey a spherical inverse-square law
lessons.investigation: An energy/momentum ledger varies aperture orientation, reflection and polarization. Accessible tables compare instantaneous and cycle-averaged quantities; no laser, high-power radiation or physical optical experiment is required.
lessons.independentChecks: Integrate sinusoidal fields over a full period, use momentum balance for incoming/outgoing waves, and compare with energy flux divided by c. Test zero transmission and both field amplitude conventions.

modules.title: Numerical evidence and a sustained investigation

lessons.title: Numerical field and circuit checks
lessons.objective: Evaluate a numerical physical prediction using independent representations, refinement and explicit numerical-versus-measurement uncertainty.
coverage: Quadrature of finite source distributions
Numerical potential gradients and separately summed fields
Mesh refinement, cancellation and singularity exclusion
Charge, power and field-law residuals
Independent analytic special cases
Finite precision, truncation and measurement bounds
Limits of apparent convergence and shared-code agreement
examples: Compare a ring-axis field integral with an analytic value across three quadrature resolutions.
Compute a potential gradient independently and expose a too-large or too-small finite-difference step.
Check a circuit solution's equation and power residuals while showing that the wrong physical model can still have tiny residuals.
misconceptions: More digits establish physical accuracy
Agreement between two views of the same calculation is independent verification
A small residual validates every model assumption
lessons.investigation: A reproducible field benchmark compares source quadrature, potential differentiation and analytic limits with exportable full-precision tables. Fixed run identifiers and stated domains preserve the evidence on reload.
lessons.independentChecks: Use independent algorithms with distinct discretizations and analytic fixtures, including near-cancellation and excluded singular geometries. Cross-check exported rows rather than only the displayed rounded summary.

lessons.title: Investigate a resonant circuit model
lessons.objective: Design, analyze and report a reproducible simulation investigation that distinguishes competing resonant-circuit models using calibrated observations and independent energy checks.
coverage: Question, prediction and controlled variables
Synthetic observation provenance and calibration
Training versus held-out frequencies
Amplitude and phase evidence with stated measurement bounds
Loss, parameter variation and instrument-loading alternatives
Identifiability, power balance and numerical checks
Reproducible saved records, uncertainty-aware conclusions and revision history
examples: Use off-resonance amplitude and phase to distinguish excess series resistance from a changed capacitor value.
Reject a candidate that matches resonance but fails held-out phase or power observations.
Write a bounded conclusion that distinguishes a supported model from proof of unique physical cause.
misconceptions: A synthetic dataset is a measured experiment
The best fit proves a unique mechanism
Calibration and validation can reuse all the same observations without qualification
lessons.investigation: The full saved project is specified in project.json. Learners record a prediction before reveal, choose informative frequency samples, compare at least two models, export evidence, and submit a self-assessed report. Practice calculations and the report remain distinct from independent quiz evidence.
lessons.independentChecks: Generate observations and verify predictions through independent real sine/cosine equations and time-averaged power, not the production phasor helper. Audit all exported observations, retained report versions and uncertainty endpoints.
